evidence: io.lisp:3503-3507: `(octets (with-open-file (in path :element-type '(unsigned-byte 8)) (let ((v (make-array (file-length in) ...))) (read-sequence v in) (coerce v 'list)))) (report (fnn-core 'fn-otm-journal-report octets))`. The path is checked with `probe-file`, which follows symlinks, and is opened through a CL stream rather than the no-follow, regular-file and bounded readers used everywhere else.
fix: Stream the journal through a guard-verified ACL2 fold, a chunk at a time, through a no-follow regular-file descriptor (as fnn-read-regular-bounded does). Alternatively read it into the octet buffer stobj and have ACL2 replay it by index; do not build a list.
reviewer: io.lisp:3503-3507 reads the whole decisions.fnj into a vector with no bound, then coerces it to a list (about 16 B per octet), and hands it to fn-otm-journal-report and again to fn-otm-journal-exit. The path is checked with probe-file and opened as a CL stream, with no nofollow, no regular-file check and no bounded reader, unlike fnn-read-regular-bounded elsewhere. It is an offline operator verb, not a served path, but the journal grows for the owner's life, so on a 2 GB node this is a real way to exhaust memory and an unbounded-work violation.
scenario: The owner appends to STORE/decisions/decisions.fnj for its whole life. With a journal of a few hundred MB, `store ROOT journal` allocates the file as a vector and then one cons per octet (about 16 B each, so roughly 16x the file size). That can exhaust the heap and fault, or push a small node (the 2 GB OpenBSD friend node) into swap. This is the octet-list representation D27 forbids on any path, and there is no admission bound. A symlinked or FIFO decisions.fnj is also followed or blocked on, unlike every other store file read.
title: `store journal` reads the whole decision journal into memory as an octet list, with no bound
